issues.legal_issue: A restricted interest held by a Hindu woman under a will, decree, or other instrument becomes absolute when it rests on a pre-existing right in the property.
material_facts: In the cases before the Court, Hindu widows received restricted interests in property under wills, compromise decrees, or court orders, including rights connected with maintenance or residence.
The women were in possession or enjoyment of the relevant property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The women or persons claiming through them later dealt with the property, and remaindermen disputed their authority to do so.
issues.conclusion: A restricted interest becomes full ownership under Section 14(1) if the woman’s interest rests on a pre-existing right; Section 14(2) applies only when the property is granted for the first time without such a right. The appeals and special leave petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(1), its Explanation, and Section 14(2) must be read as an integral scheme. Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1) and applies to a first-time grant made without a pre-existing right. The Court followed Badri Prasad v. Smt. Kanso Devi, V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy, and Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, among other consistent authorities. It distinguished Mst. Karmi v. Amru as not deciding the scope of Section 14(1) and (2).

issues.definition: When a civil property dispute concerns a Hindu woman who received a restricted interest based on a pre-existing property right and possessed or enjoyed the property when the law changed, she holds it as absolute owner.

issues.legal_issue: Applying a change in law to enlarge a Hindu woman’s pre-existing restricted interest in property is not retrospective merely because the instrument creating that interest predates the change.
material_facts: The interests at issue were created by instruments or arrangements made before the relevant change in law.
The women’s restricted interests were connected to pre-existing rights and the women possessed or enjoyed the property when the change took effect.
The challenge to enlargement of the interests relied on the fact that the instruments predated the change in law.
issues.conclusion: The application of Section 14(1) to enlarge a restricted interest supported by a pre-existing right is not retrospective; it applies the law to the woman’s position when the law took effect. A stranger legatee remains bound by the restrictions in the instrument.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) is not retroactive. Devolution under a will takes effect after the testator’s death, and a legatee is ordinarily bound by its restrictions. But applying the law to the facts existing when it came into force is not retrospective where a Hindu woman had a pre-existing right and possessed the property; the law then enlarges her limited interest. The Court relied on the principles in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy and the related authorities discussed in its judgment.
